name: Maya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, finished secondary school and am still a junior claims clerk learning the policy wording. I use AI every day to sort scanned receipts, but I ask a senior clerk about unusual exclusions. My partner Dev drives a bus, we have two children in school and a mortgage. My pay is low for this job, we have less than a month of expenses saved and there are few similar offices nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the claims desk that a small filing improvement helps me find missing documents before lunch. I already use AI every day to group scanned receipts, but I still check policy dates because I am learning this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am a junior clerk on low pay with a secondary-school education, and I still ask the senior clerk about unusual exclusions. My partner Dev drives a bus, we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and our savings would not cover a full month of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my daily receipt checks and put 15 a week in a separate account only when both current wages cover the mortgage and groceries. In the first year I would use the same scanner tool and mark its mistaken dates before sending a claim on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even in this quiet picture, because one missed shift would make the mortgage tight. The scan saves minutes; it does not make the payment at month end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake did you catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clinic receipt showed a visit outside the policy dates, but the scanner placed it with the covered dates. I caught it only because I compared the stamped day with the policy start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where are you still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the senior clerk to show me the exclusion once more. I am quick with software, but still slow with some of the policy wording.

say: I would keep **date checks** beside daily AI receipt sorting.
I would ask **senior clerks** about unfamiliar exclusions.
think: I have **under one month saved** against a mortgage and two children.
I remain **junior and learning** despite daily AI use.
do: **Check scanned receipts** each day against policy dates.
**Set aside 15 weekly** only while both wages cover food and mortgage.
S0.quote: The scan saves minutes; it does not make the payment at month end.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** speeds filing but does not replace policy knowledge.
The **thin reserve** makes baseline mortgage pressure real before any major AI change.

steps.text: Check scanned claim receipts daily against signed policy dates
Save 15 weekly only while both wages cover mortgage and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say Steady Disruption could let software answer routine claim questions and check far more receipts than I do. I would ask for paid time to learn the new checking screen, because my job could shrink before I become good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think junior hours might be cut first, but I do not know the manager’s plan. Dev’s bus wage alone would not cover the mortgage, food and school costs, and there are few insurers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask this month for one paid hour with a senior clerk learning the new denial checker, with my normal shifts protected. If approved I would practise on invented claims; if my hours actually fall I would ask nearby offices about posted paid vacancies and cut weekend takeaways first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, but learning the screen is something I can do. A course after an unpaid shift is no help to our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the paid hour agreed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need written approval for the paid hour; the firm has not offered it. If the answer is no, I would keep the current rota and ask the senior clerk to flag changes during paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another job viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would only apply to a real posted job with take-home pay after travel that covers the gap in our household budget. A vacancy at the far office can cost more in fares than it adds in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that AGI by 2028 could read policies, check receipts and answer customers for less than our junior team costs. Robots doing hands-on visits might follow around 2031, but our screen work faces the 2028 date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior claims job to end, and I lie awake adding the mortgage to the children’s school costs. We have less than one month saved; Dev’s current bus wage cannot cover everything alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written cut dates now and put the small reserve toward mortgage and food, not another device. If the job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for actual paid local office openings only if qualified take-home pay after travel closes our household budget gap; I would check public-help eligibility, not count it early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing my own wage before we can build any cushion. The mortgage letter will not wait while I learn a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen another office offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen a local office offer yet, and AGI could shrink those roles too. I would ask for salary, hours and training requirements before spending money on an application trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could public help cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the support office to ask what our household qualifies for. I cannot tell the children it will pay for school until that is confirmed.

I have **under one month saved** for the mortgage.

steps.text: Request written cut dates and preserve reserve for mortgage and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives my family some years to try a different skill while the claims wage still arrives. Robots that handle physical work might follow around 2034, so I would not call any hands-on job safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like learning new software, but a course fee would take food money today. I would consider medical reception only if a clinic offers a paid supervised place and shows its qualification rules; AGI may reach booking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two nearby clinics for actual paid supervised openings and written training requirements, then ask my insurer for protected paid hours to try one shift. If those conditions hold and our net income after travel covers mortgage, food, school costs and other basic bills, I would train; after 2031 job loss I would apply only to a qualified paid opening that still exists and passes the same budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though the five-year window lets me check a route without giving up a wage first. An unpaid trial is a bill, not a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are those shifts secured?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic has not offered me a shift and the insurer has not protected my hours. If either refuses, I would stay in the paid claims rota and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would clinic work survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clinic desk may also use AGI for booking and records. I would ask which paid duties remain before taking the children through a house move.

I would protect **current claims shifts** before trying clinic work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to make the claims job less fragile and save what we can. Hands-on robots may follow around 2039, after the screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The date is far away, but my mortgage is due next month and our reserve is still under one month. I cannot feel calm about our income just because the technology arrives later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep daily receipt checks and put 10 a week into the reserve only when both current wages cover food, school costs and the mortgage. I would ask the manager yearly about paid training and posted roles; if my job ends after 2036 I would apply only where I qualify and take-home household pay after fares covers bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household now, even with ten years before AGI. The longer calendar does not create a spare month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the paid training has protected shifts and a real role at the end. If there is only a certificate, I would keep my current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can Dev’s wage be projected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask Dev to promise the same bus hours ten years from now. We would redo the budget from the wages we actually have each year.

I would keep **receipt date checks** while working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my junior wage to end with almost no cash to carry the mortgage. Written cut notice, real qualified paid work with household pay after fares covering bills and confirmed public eligibility would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how often I check the mortgage account. I open the bank app before the children wake up on payday.

headlineQuote: I open the bank app before the children wake up on payday.
portrait: Maya is a **43-year-old junior claims clerk** with secondary school education, low pay and daily AI use.
She and Dev have **two schoolchildren**, a mortgage and under one month of expenses saved.
She learns **policy dates and exclusions** while using AI to sort scanned receipts.
She asks for **paid protected training** and applies only to real qualified jobs covering household bills after travel.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before the household has a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, real bill-covering paid work and confirmed public eligibility would help.
